211.title: Vayigash: he drew near (Genesis 44:18)
211.hook: Judah steps forward; the portion's name means "he approached"
211.howItsDone: Vayigash is read in synagogue in winter, in early winter; its opening scene of Judah pleading for Benjamin is often taught as the moment the brothers' story turns from betrayal toward repair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph slipped out of the room to cry, washed his face, and walked back in. Your line was wash your face, go back. Today we're still in that room, and someone finally moves.

The silver cup has been found in Benjamin's sack. The brothers have torn their clothes and trudged back to the city. The ruler of Egypt, their brother Joseph, though they still don't know it, gives his verdict: the one with the cup stays here as my slave. The rest of you, go home in peace. Everyone is frozen, like a meeting where the boss has spoken and nobody breathes. It would be easy to look at the floor and let it happen. Then one man steps forward.
screen: `THE CUP IN BENJAMIN'S SACK.` → `THE RULER'S VERDICT.` → `ONE MAN STEPS FORWARD.`

segments.voice: This week's portion is named for its first word, vayigash: and he drew near. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "Then Judah came near unto him." Judah walks up to the man who rules Egypt for Pharaoh, close enough to speak into his ear, and asks to be heard. Remember who Judah is. Years earlier, with Joseph in the pit, it was Judah who said, let's sell him. Now he's the one who won't leave a brother behind. What follows is a long speech. Judah tells the whole story: our old father, the son he lost, the youngest son he barely let us take. If we come home without the boy, our father will die of grief. Then the offer. Keep me instead. Let me stay as your slave, and let the boy go home with his brothers. The rabbis looked hard at that little verb. A midrash says a person can draw near for three reasons: to fight, to make peace, or to pray. Judah, they say, came ready for all three: firm enough to argue, gentle enough to plead, humble enough to hope. The word Jew goes back, through the tribe and later the kingdom of Judah, to his name, Yehudah. In a real sense, the people carry the name of the brother who stepped forward. Before anything in this family can be repaired, somebody has to walk across the room.

212.title: Vayigash: does my father live? (Genesis 45:3)
212.hook: Joseph's first words after "I am Joseph" are about his father
212.tomorrow: Vayigash: don't fall out on the way
212.howItsDone: Honoring father and mother is one of the Ten Commandments, and Jewish law spells it out in practical ways: providing for aging parents, standing when they enter, not contradicting them harshly, and saying Kaddish for them after they die.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judah drew near and offered himself in place of his youngest brother. Your line was draw near. Today, the man he was pleading with breaks.

Judah has just finished speaking. He's described an old man at home who will die of grief if the youngest son doesn't come back. And the ruler of Egypt can't hold it in anymore. He clears the room: everyone out. The servants go. Now it's only him and his brothers. He cries so loudly the Egyptians hear it through the walls. Then he says two sentences. The first is the line people know. The second one is today.

In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" In Hebrew it's five words. Ani Yosef, I am Joseph. Ha'od avi chai, is my father still alive? The brothers can't answer; they're terrified in front of him. Here's the puzzle the rabbis loved. Joseph already knows the answer: Judah's whole speech was about their living father. So why ask? One answer: it isn't a question for information. It's the first thing out of a son who hasn't seen his father since the day he was sold. The power, the grain, the revenge he could take all fall away, and what's left is: Dad. Is he really alive? Another answer is sharper. Some readers hear a rebuke underneath. You talk about our father's grief, Judah? Where was that concern the day you sold me? A midrash says that when the brothers couldn't answer this one question, a sage later sighed: if a brother's words left them speechless, how will any of us answer on the day we're asked about our own lives? Both readings can be true at once. Then Joseph says, come near to me, please. The same verb as yesterday. Judah drew near to plead; now Joseph asks all of them to draw near to be forgiven. The first thing a lost son asks about is the parent. Joseph waited years to ask it out loud. Some people wait longer than they meant to.

213.title: Vayigash: don't fall out on the way (Genesis 45:24)
213.hook: Joseph sends his brothers home: "See that ye fall not out by the way"
213.carry: don't fall out on the way
213.howItsDone: Jews traditionally say the traveler's prayer, Tefillat HaDerech, when setting out on a journey beyond their town, asking for a safe road and a peaceful return.

segments.voice: Yesterday: I am Joseph, and in the same breath, doth my father yet live. Today, Joseph sends his brothers home to fetch that father, with one piece of advice for the road.

Some family car rides go like this. The wedding is over, or the funeral, or the big talk, and now everyone's in the car together for three hours, and all the things nobody said in the room are sitting in the back seat. Joseph's brothers are about to take that ride. They've just learned the brother they sold is alive and running Egypt. They're loaded with grain and gifts, heading home to tell their father. And somebody, at some point on that road, is going to say: this was your idea.
screen: `THE LONG RIDE HOME.` → `WHAT NOBODY SAID IN THE ROOM.` → `THIS WAS YOUR IDEA.`

segments.voice: Joseph sees it coming. He loads them with wagons and food. He gives each brother a change of clothes, and Benjamin, pointedly, three hundred pieces of silver and five changes. Then, at the door, one line. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "See that ye fall not out by the way." In Hebrew, al tirgezu ba-derech: don't get stirred up on the road. What is he worried about? Rashi, the medieval commentator, says: don't quarrel about me. Don't spend the trip arguing over who said sell him and who went along. The past is settled; don't reopen it on the highway. The Talmud offers a funnier, gentler reading: don't get so deep into a Torah argument on the road that you miss your turn. And take normal steps, and get into town before dark. Practical travel advice from a brother who knows the route. A third reader, Rashbam, hears the verb differently. It can mean to tremble, so he reads it as: don't be afraid on the way. You're not in trouble anymore. And the Talmud raises one more eyebrow, at those five sets of clothes for Benjamin. Didn't one special coat start this whole disaster? The sages ask the question honestly. Put the readings together: the fight's over. Don't restart it, don't get lost in it, and don't carry the fear home with you.

214.title: Vayigash: the wagons (Genesis 45:26–28)
214.hook: Jacob can't believe it until he sees the wagons, then his spirit revives
214.howItsDone: Jewish tradition has blessings for news: on hearing good news that benefits others too, many say the blessing praising God who is good and does good, and on hard news they say the blessing for the true Judge.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph's advice for the ride home: don't fall out on the way. Today the brothers arrive, and they have to tell their father the news.

Some news is too good to believe. The phone call that says the test came back clear. The text from someone you thought you'd lost touch with forever. Your first reaction isn't joy. It's: no, that can't be right. Now picture an old man who has grieved a son for over twenty years. He was shown a bloody coat. He said he'd go down to his grave mourning. And his sons walk in and say: Joseph is alive. He's the ruler of all Egypt.
screen: `TOO GOOD TO BELIEVE.` → `AN OLD MAN AND A BLOODY COAT.` → `JOSEPH IS ALIVE.`

segments.voice: The first reaction, the text says, is that Jacob's heart went numb. He didn't believe them. Words weren't enough. So the brothers tell him everything Joseph said. Then he sees the wagons Joseph had sent from Egypt to carry him down. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "the spirit of Jacob their father revived." Then he speaks. "It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive; I will go and see him before I die." Why the wagons? The rabbis noticed a pun. The Hebrew for wagons, agalot, sounds like eglah, a young cow. Rashi passes on a tradition that the last thing Jacob and Joseph studied together, before Joseph vanished, was a passage about a heifer. So the wagons were a private signal only a father would understand: it's really me, and I remember. Later storytellers add a tender scene the Torah doesn't have: Asher's daughter, Serach, breaks the news to her grandfather gently, in a song, so the shock won't hurt him. The Torah itself is silent about how they told him. And watch one small thing. In the verse where his spirit revives, he's still Jacob. In the very next verse, when he decides to go, the text calls him Israel, his larger name. Rashi adds that the presence of God, which had left him in his grief, came back. Sometimes good news needs to be seen before it can be believed. And sometimes the person delivering it matters as much as the news.

segments.voice: Think of one piece of good news you're holding that someone else would love to hear: a thank-you you haven't passed on, a compliment said behind their back, their kid did well, the thing they worried about worked out. 215.title: Vayigash: few and evil days (Genesis 47:9)
215.hook: asked his age, Jacob tells Pharaoh his years have been hard
215.howItsDone: Honest lament has a long home in Jewish prayer, from the Psalms and the Book of Lamentations, read on Tisha b'Av, to the custom of speaking openly about the dead and one's loss during the week of shiva.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vayigash: the wagons, and an old father who finally believes. His spirit revived. Today, the last scene of this portion: that old father meets the king of Egypt.

How are you? Good! Fine. Busy. It's the standard answer at the coffee machine, even in a year when a marriage is ending, or a parent is sick, or the work has dried up. A small social lie, and an easy one. Now an elderly shepherd, just arrived in a foreign country, stands before the king of Egypt. The king makes polite conversation: how old are you? Jacob could say a number and smile. He doesn't.
screen: `GOOD! FINE. BUSY.` → `A SHEPHERD BEFORE A KING.` → `HOW OLD ARE YOU?`

segments.voice: Joseph brings his father to meet Pharaoh. Jacob blesses the king, an old man blessing a ruler, which already tells you something. Pharaoh asks, roughly, how many years have you lived? Jacob answers: a hundred and thirty years of wandering. And then, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "few and evil" have been the days of my life, and they haven't reached the years of my fathers. In Hebrew, me'at v'ra'im. Few and hard. Think about what he's carrying. He fled a brother who wanted to kill him. His father-in-law cheated him for twenty years. His beloved Rachel died on the road. His daughter Dinah was violated. For years he believed his favorite son was dead. That's the honest summary, and he gives it to a king. Commentators disagree about this answer. Some admire it: no pretending, not even before Pharaoh. Others think he complained to the wrong person at the wrong moment, just after his son was found alive. A medieval tradition even counts the words of the conversation and says each word of complaint cost him a year. Jacob lives to a hundred and forty-seven, fewer than his father or grandfather. Either way, the Torah keeps the answer. It lets a patriarch say out loud: my life has been hard. And then it lets him bless the king anyway, on his way out.
screen: `AN OLD MAN BLESSES A KING.` · `A HUNDRED AND THIRTY YEARS.` · `ME'AT V'RA'IM — FEW AND HARD.` · `ADMIRED BY SOME, FAULTED BY OTHERS.` · then, large: `HONEST ABOUT THE YEARS.`

segments.voice: Find one stretch of your own years that was genuinely hard, one you usually sum up as fine, and name it to yourself plainly, the way Jacob did: that year was hard. No drama, no fixing. Then, if you can, find one thing from it you'd still bless, the way Jacob blessed the king on his way out.

216.title: Vayechi: and he lived
216.hook: the portion of Jacob's death is called "and he lived"
216.carry: the death portion is called life
216.howItsDone: Some Jews write an ethical will, a letter to their children about the values they hope to pass on, a custom some trace to Jacob's last words to his sons in this portion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of Vayigash: Jacob tells Pharaoh his days have been few and hard. Honest about the years. Today, a new portion, the last one in Genesis.

A hospital wing is named for a donor. A scholarship is named for someone who died young. A baby is named for a grandmother. The name tells you what somebody wanted remembered. The final portion of Genesis tells of Jacob's last days: he gathers his sons, gives his blessings, asks to be buried, and dies. It's a deathbed portion from start to finish. And its name is: and he lived.
screen: `WHAT A NAME REMEMBERS.` → `A DEATHBED PORTION.` → `CALLED AND HE LIVED.`

segments.voice: Like the other portions, this one is named for an early word. The first verse, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And Jacob lived in the land of Egypt seventeen years." Vayechi: and he lived. You may remember this pattern. The portion about Sarah's death is called Chayei Sarah, the life of Sarah. A portion that tells of a death carries a word of life in its name. Readers noticed the number too. Joseph had seventeen years with his father before he was sold. Now his father gets seventeen years with him, in Egypt. The years come back around. Rashi notices something on the page. In a handwritten Torah scroll, a new portion begins after a little blank space. This one doesn't. It runs straight on from the last line, closed. Rashi gives two reasons. With Jacob's death, the hard years of Egypt began to press in, and the people's hearts felt shut. Or: Jacob wanted to tell his sons the end of days, and that vision was closed to him. Then the boldest line. The Talmud records Rabbi Yochanan saying: Jacob our father did not die. His students object: he was embalmed and buried! Rabbi Yochanan answers from scripture: as long as his children are alive, he's alive. So the death portion is called life. Not because death isn't real, but because what a person hands on keeps living in the people after them.

217.title: Vayechi: true kindness (Genesis 47:29)
217.hook: kindness to the dead is called true kindness, since it can't be repaid
217.howItsDone: Many Jewish communities have a chevra kadisha, a volunteer burial society that prepares the dead with ritual washing and simple shrouds, and at funerals mourners and friends often help fill the grave themselves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vayechi: the death portion is called life. This week, Judah drew near, Joseph asked after his father and sent his brothers off without a fight, the wagons revived Jacob, and Jacob told a king the truth. Today, Jacob's last request.

A lot of everyday kindness has a little loop in it. I help you move; someday you'll help me. I bring soup when you're sick; you'll remember. That's not a bad thing. It's how friendships and neighborhoods work. But one kind of help has a loop that can't close. The person you're helping will never thank you, never return the favor, never even know. Near the end, Jacob asks his son for exactly that kind of help.
screen: `A LITTLE LOOP IN KINDNESS.` → `HELP THAT CAN'T BE RETURNED.` → `JACOB'S LAST REQUEST.`

segments.voice: Jacob knows he's dying. He calls Joseph, asks him to swear an oath, and says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "deal kindly and truly with me; bury me not, I pray thee, in Egypt." Take me home. Bury me with my fathers in the cave they bought, in the land that was promised. In Hebrew, kindly and truly is chesed ve'emet. Kindness and truth. Rashi gives it a name. Kindness done for the dead, he says, is chesed shel emet, true kindness. Why true? Because the one you do it for can never pay you back. No loop, no thank-you note coming. Kindness with nothing mixed in. Jewish communities built that idea into an institution: a volunteer group called the chevra kadisha, the holy society. Its members gently wash the body of someone who has died, dress them in simple white shrouds, and sit with them so they're never left alone before the funeral. The work happens out of sight, and the one they serve can never thank them. At a traditional burial, mourners and friends take turns shoveling earth into the grave themselves. It's heavy, hard, and nobody can repay it. That's the point. And Joseph keeps his oath. When Jacob dies, Joseph and his brothers carry him all the way back to the cave and bury him there. True kindness, delivered.
screen: `DEAL KINDLY AND TRULY WITH ME.` · `CHESED SHEL EMET — TRUE KINDNESS.` · `THE HOLY SOCIETY.` · `JOSEPH KEEPS HIS OATH.` · then, large: `KINDNESS THAT CAN'T BE REPAID.`

Choose one you could actually do, and picture doing it and walking away without a word.
Chesed ve'emet. Kindness and truth: Jacob's request to Joseph, which Rashi read as true kindness because it could never be paid back.
